item.title: Parameterized Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Efficient Simulation of Embedded Microfluidic Chip Cooling
item.description: arXiv:2611.10666v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Embedded microfluidic cooling is a promising technology for dissipating the intense heat generated by high-performance electronic chips. However, the design and optimization of such coolers impose prohibitive computational costs when using conventional numerical solvers. Here, we present a parameterized physics-informed neural network (PINN) as a deep learning framework for rapidly and accurately predicting the thermohydraulic performance of embedded manifold microchannels. By incorporating four geometric dimensions along with three spatial coordinates as the network inputs, the proposed model enables multiphysics prediction across a continuous design space. Remarkably, our predicted velocity and temperature fields differ from finite-element simulations by relative errors of only 8.1% and 5.6%, respectively, while reducing the computational time and cost by over four orders of magnitude. Key to this framework is a composite strategy combining geometric ansatz embedding, the SOAP optimizer, and a thermal-conductivity-based curriculum learning scheme, which helps overcome the convergence challenges inherent in training PINNs for complex three-dimensional flows. Notably, by leveraging a highly optimized JAX backend, the network achieves convergence on a single consumer-grade GPU in less than four hours. Our approach offers a physics-consistent, real-time surrogate model that can substantially accelerate innovations in advanced microfluidic cooling of future electronics.
item.dc:creator: Weiheng Li, Zhiyao Jiang, Bai Song

item.title: Bifurcation-based phononic frequency combs in a forced van der Pol-Duffing oscillator
item.description: arXiv:2611.10722v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Here, we analyze the dynamics of a forced Van der Pol-Duffing oscillator in search of phononic frequency comb (PFC) generation. When the drive amplitude is small, quasi-periodic self-oscillations are dominant, and we obtain a PFC spectrum response of the oscillator. When the drive amplitude is sufficiently large, we obtain frequency locking. We observe that near the transition to frequency locking the PFC spectrum is strongest and has more peaks. With increasing drive amplitude, the peaks coalesce, and the PFC spectrum disappears at an infinite-period saddle-node or homoclinic bifurcation. We also study the stability of the frequency-locked responses and find that a PFC spectrum can also occur near a subcritical Hopf bifurcation. We find that the first-order averaged equations of our nonlinear dynamical system are identical to the equations of motion of the Stuart-Landau oscillator. We use averaging techniques up to second order to characterize the quasi-periodic solutions. Very good agreement with numerical integration results are obtained. We complement our analysis by proposing a phenomenological model of nonlinear dissipative coupling between two modes that accounts for the negative dissipation term in the van der Pol-Duffing equation of motion.
item.dc:creator: Adriano A. Batista, Madhurendra Mishra, Adarsh Ganesan

item.title: Demonstration of High fmax (> 80 GHz) in Recessed-Gate and Passivated $\mathrm{Al_{0.60}Ga_{0.40}N}$ Channel RF HEMTs
item.description: arXiv:2611.11037v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this work, ultra-wide bandgap (UWBG) $\mathrm{Al_{0.60}Ga_{0.40}N}$ channel high-electron-mobility transistors (HEMTs) with an $\mathrm{Al_{0.81}Ga_{0.19}N}$ barrier and an $\mathrm{Al_{0.86}Ga_{0.14}N}$ back barrier were fabricated. The devices featured a recessed T-gate structure and $\mathrm{SiO_2}$ passivation. Scaled devices achieved a cutoff frequency ($f_{\mathrm{T}}$) of 35 GHz, a maximum oscillation frequency ($f_{\mathrm{max}}$) of 82 GHz, and an average breakdown field $> 3 \mathrm{MV/cm}$, while maintaining a reasonable current collapse of $\sim 20\%$ under a 40 V drain bias in pinch-off condition. Devices with larger dimensions demonstrated a high off-state breakdown voltage of 883 V and an $f_{\mathrm{T}}$ of 24 GHz, yielding a high Johnson's figure of merit ($\mathrm{JFOM}$) of 21.19 $\mathrm{THz \cdot V}$. Across all device geometries, a high $I_{\mathrm{ON}}/I_{\mathrm{OFF}}$ ratio exceeding $10^6$ was observed with drain and gate leakage currents strictly below $10^{-6} \mathrm{A/mm}$. This work demonstrates an optimized design for $\mathrm{AlGaN}$ channel RF HEMTs and their excellent potential for X- to Ka-band applications.
item.dc:creator: Meherab Hossain, Ruixin Bai, Swarnav Mukhopadhyay, Brahmani Challa, Guangying Wang, Surjava Sanyal, Md Tahmidul Alam, Khush Gohel, Rafael A. Choudhury, Shubhra S. Pasayat, Chirag Gupta

item.title: $>3\text{ W/mm}$ Output Power $\mathrm{Al}_{0.61}\mathrm{Ga}_{0.39}\mathrm{N}$ Channel HEMT with $24.4\%$ Associated PAE at $10\text{ GHz}$
item.description: arXiv:2611.11042v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this work, an ultra-wide bandgap (UWBG) high-electron-mobility transistor (HEMT) was fabricated using an $\mathrm{Al}_{0.76}\mathrm{Ga}_{0.24}\mathrm{N}$ barrier and an $\mathrm{Al}_{0.61}\mathrm{Ga}_{0.39}\mathrm{N}$ channel with thick $\mathrm{SiO}_2$ passivation. The device demonstrated low current collapse at $40\text{ V}$ drain bias. At $10\text{ GHz}$, the device exhibited an output power of $3.07\text{ W/mm}$ with an associated power-added efficiency (PAE) of $24.4\%$. A peak PAE of $33.9\%$ was achieved at an associated output power of $2.14\text{ W/mm}$. This excellent large-signal performance highlights the strong potential of UWBG $\mathrm{AlGaN}$ channel devices for X-band applications.
item.dc:creator: Meherab Hossain, Ruixin Bai, Swarnav Mukhopadhyay, Brahmani Challa, Kuan Chang Pan, Ryan Gilbert, Guangying Wang, Surjava Sanyal, Chuang Ye, Md Tahmidul Alam, Khush Gohel, Ahmad E. Islam, Andrew J. Green, Shubhra S. Pasayat, Chirag Gupta

item.title: Extreme temperatures characterization of Al0.6Ga0.4N channel HEMT
item.description: arXiv:2611.11524v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this work, we fabricate and characterize ultra-wide bandgap Al0.6Ga0.4N channel HEMTs with Pt/Au gate under a wide temperature range of 20 K to 650 K. The devices retained robust modulation capability throughout the measurement, with excellent on/off ratio of 9.7 * 107 and 6.4 * 107 under 20 K and 650 K. The DC output IV measurement was performed, with Id,max of a device with Lsd = 9 {\mu}m measured to be 240 mA/mm and 120 mA/mm under 20 K and 650 K. In addition, low drain and leakage were observed in multiple devices, and the device robustness was evaluated under room temperature after the extreme temperature measurement with minimal degradation observed in Id,max and Rsheet. Moreover, transfer I-V characteristics of the Al0.6Ga0.4N channel HEMTs have also been studied, where a relatively small Vth shift was observed. TLM measurement and transconductance analysis both indicate the presence of weak temperature dependent scattering mechanisms in the device channel. The subthreshold swing (SS) was calculated and observed to increase parallelly to SSideal under investigated temperature, indicates a robust gate structure. Finally, the on/off ratio and Ig of the 9 {\mu}m Lsd device were benchmarked and compared favorably against other reported results. While the results offer insight into the extreme temperature performance of AlGaN channel HEMT with Al composition higher than 50%, it also establishes AlGaN channel HEMT as a promising candidate for extreme temperature electronic applications.
item.dc:creator: Shuwen Xie, Jacklyn Zhu, Swarnav Mukhopadhyay, Yi-Chen Liu, Shubhra Pasayat, Savannah Eisner, Chirag Gupta

item.title: Split-Ring Couplers for On-Skin Wi-Fi Communication via an SSPP Waveguide Textile
item.description: arXiv:2611.12036v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Textile spoof surface plasmon polariton (SSPP) waveguides offer guided on-body links, but their body-facing ground conductors obstruct coupling from on-skin wireless nodes. This letter presents a split-ring coupling interface using local ground recesses at the textile terminations, without patterned garment-side launchers. The capacitively loaded rings are supported by polydimethylsiloxane carriers with a thickness of 2~mm. An image-current model and full-wave simulations examine the effect of backing-ground spacing and determine the recess geometry. For a 450~mm textile waveguide on a water-filled body phantom, the measured $S_{21}$ at 2.45 GHz was $-$18.8~dB, versus $-$60.9~dB without the textile. A 625-position scan showed a maximum 5.1 dB reduction relative to the nominal position within the measured joint $\pm$5~mm placement region. A separate two-node IEEE~802.11n test demonstrated a 65~Mb/s physical-layer (PHY) rate with zero packet errors among 300 frames at $-$20~dBm transmit power through the coupler link. These results establish high-rate, placement-tolerant on-skin Wi-Fi communication through an SSPP waveguide textile.
item.dc:creator: Akihito Noda, Ryo Takahashi

item.title: Analytical Framework Relating Capacitance-Frequency Measurements and Hysteresis in Perovskite Solar Cells
item.description: arXiv:2611.12115v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mobile ion migration strongly influences the electrical response and current-voltage hysteresis of perovskite solar cells. However, quantitative determination of ionic transport parameters typically requires transient measurements, extensive numerical simulations, and/or fitting procedures involving multiple uncertain parameters. Here, we present an analytical model that establishes a direct relationship between capacitance-frequency (C-f) characteristics and ionic transport properties in perovskite solar cells, while accounting for interlayer effects. The model describes the transition from the ion-screened depletion capacitance at low frequencies to the geometric capacitance at high frequencies and demonstrates that the characteristic transition frequency provides a direct measure of the dielectric relaxation time for ions. Furthermore, the model establishes a quantitative connection between C-f characteristics and scan-rate-dependent current-voltage hysteresis, enabling prediction of the scan-rate window in which maximum hysteresis occurs. Drift-diffusion simulations show excellent agreement with the analytical predictions over wide ranges of ion density, ion mobility, transport-layer mobility and doping concentration. Experimental measurements confirm the predicted correlation between capacitance and hysteresis. By providing a direct, physically transparent, and computationally efficient route for extracting ionic transport parameters from routine impedance measurements, this work offers a practical tool for quantifying ion migration and understanding dynamic phenomena in perovskite solar cells.
item.dc:creator: Manjeet Kumar, Changzeng Ding, Mathias Nyman, Yongqi Sun, Chang-Qi Ma, Ronald \"Osterbacka, Oskar J. Sandberg

item.title: Mechanisms of Zener diode and ohmic contact resulting from a heavily doped p-n junction: A novel explanation in terms of impurity-photovoltaic-effect resulting from infrared self-emission at room-temperature
item.description: arXiv:2611.12431v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In textbooks, a quantum-mechanical tunneling mechanism based on electron-wavefunction is used to explain Zener diode as well as ohmic contact resulting from a heavily doped p-n junction. In this study, an attempt in particle description is made to explain these devices. Any object at room-temperature emits infrared (IR) photons. The process of heavy doping can cause many defects. The self-absorption of the IR emission could be achieved through sub-band-gap excitations due to defects, creating carriers. In a heavily doped p-n junction device, some of the IR-generated carriers diffuse into the junction which has a built-in field. The built-in field sweeps out the carriers, creating IR photocurrent. The reverse leakage current of the p-n junction is regarded as the IR photocurrent according to a precedent where impurity-photovoltaic-effect is used to explain circuit devices (arXiv:2510.18226). Heavy doping results in not only a great many IR-generated carriers but also an avalanche effect at low voltage, producing Zener breakdown. Additionally, the impurity-photovoltaic-effect can make a reasonable contribution to explaining the temperature dependence of Zener breakdown. If the doping is very heavy, the heavily doped p-n junction can be altered to create an ohmic contact, which can also be explained in terms of impurity-photovoltaic-effect. Not only quantum mechanics, but also this photovoltaic mechanism in particle description can explain the above devices. Considering the wave-particle duality, the combination of quantum-mechanical and photovoltaic mechanisms is suggested to explain these devices. Each mechanism plays a big or small role in the explanation.
item.dc:creator: Jianming Li

item.title: Neutronic Field-Effect Transistor
item.description: arXiv:2611.12651v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Field-effect electronic devices are in widespread use in communication, computing, data storage, and sensing applications. We demonstrate a neutronic field-effect transistor (NFET) that is analogous to the Datta-Das electron spin transistor and atomtronic devices. The NFET is based on a perfect-crystal Mach-Zehnder neutron interferometer with phase shifts applied to the spin and path degrees of freedom.
item.dc:creator: Dusan Sarenac, Charles W. Clark, Owen Lailey, Muhammad Arif, Wangchun Chen, David G. Cory, Michael G. Huber, Joachim Nsofini, Dmitry A. Pushin

item.title: The Weight Is in the Reading: Hidden States in Memristors, Memlumors, and Electrochemical Transistors
item.description: arXiv:2611.12706v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Physical synapses are routinely described by a single number, the weight, that is identified with a conductance, a current, or a luminescence yield. This identification conflates two different objects: the internal state that the device stores, and the signal obtained when that state is read. Building on Chua's formulation of memristive systems, we separate the state variable, which evolves with the excitation history, from the observation map that converts it into a measured signal, and we define the weight as the outcome of a specified read protocol. Three platforms show the consequences: a memristor, in which the same voltage writes and reads; a memlumor, in which light both modifies the state and produces the photoluminescence that reports it; and an organic electrochemical transistor (OECT), in which the gate writes and the channel reads. In the transistor, two states prepared by different histories give the same channel current at a specific drain bias and become distinguishable again when the bias is changed, while the stored charge persists and the gate current continues to separate them. Published experiments provide precedents: a drain-bias-dependent cancellation of the OECT transient, and trapped charges in perovskite memlumors that are invisible to conventional time-resolved photoluminescence but revealed by a read-write-read sequence. A synaptic weight is therefore not a property of the material alone but of the material together with its readout, and reports of synaptic behavior should specify what is stored, what is measured, and how one is inferred from the other.
item.dc:creator: Gonzalo Rivera-Sierra, Heyi Zhang, Daiki Nishioka, Takashi Tsuchiya, Juan Bisquert

item.title: Manufacturing Complex Structures Through Interfacial Self-Organization
item.description: arXiv:2611.09950v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Conventional manufacturing constructs three-dimensional geometries through localized material deposition, removal, or shaping, with fabrication effort greatly increasing with geometric complexity. Here, we introduce a manufacturing approach in which target geometry is encoded into sparse wireframe scaffolds that guide liquid self-organization through interfacial forces. We apply a computational framework that approximates arbitrary target geometries using constant-mean-curvature surface domains and extracts their boundaries to construct the scaffolds. Under neutral buoyancy conditions, curable liquids injected into these scaffolds self-organize into the prescribed geometries, which are subsequently solidified into mechanically isotropic structures with optically smooth surfaces. We demonstrate the fabrication of complex anatomical models and topology-optimized structures featuring intricate branching geometries, internal cavities, and integrated materials. This approach opens new possibilities for scalable fabrication of complex geometric designs.
item.dc:creator: Jacob Garrett, Abhinit Sati, Edward Chien, Emily Whiting, Valeri Frumkin

item.title: Physics in Safety and Safety in Physics: Lessons from the LHC and its Underground Experiments
item.description: arXiv:2611.10041v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large underground particle-physics facilities are usually discussed by separating scientific performance from the systems that make their operation safe. We develop a complementary view in which safety is treated as an intrinsic part of the physical and operational structure of an experiment. Using the LHC, ATLAS, and CMS as principal case studies, we introduce the concepts of physics in safety and safety in physics: physical laws, measurements, and models determine hazards and protective barriers, while those barriers in turn define the machine, detector, access, and intervention states in which physics can be performed. We formulate this relation through a \emph{safe operational phase space} and through admissible trajectories connecting different configurations, emphasizing that safety constrains not only states but also transitions between them. The framework is applied to beam and magnet protection, cryogenic and oxygen-deficiency hazards, detector-specific risk configurations, personnel access, maintenance, and radiation protection, with particular attention to the different architectures of ATLAS and CMS. We argue that validated protection does not merely restrict scientific activity but can enlarge the domain of sustainable operation. This viewpoint provides a unified physical and operational framework for understanding safety at the LHC and for incorporating protection, maintainability, and recoverability into the design of future accelerator and underground facilities such as HL-LHC, FCC and muon collider.
item.dc:creator: Alexander S. Sakharov

item.title: Exceptional Topological Bound States in the Continuum
item.description: arXiv:2611.10077v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Topological phases, exceptional points, and bound states in the continuum (BICs) are three key concepts in condensed matter and classical wave physics. Their pairwise combinations have yielded a rich variety of intriguing singular modes, but the triple merger--exceptional topological BICs (ET-BICs)--has yet to be explored. In this Letter, we theoretically propose and experimentally demonstrate a universal approach for constructing such elusive exceptional structures. The system consists of four coupled topological chains: y-mirror stacking generates pairs of topological BICs, while z-stacking with biased loss yields a generalized mirror symmetry under which each pair--separated in different subspaces until their collapse--merges into an ET-BIC at a critical loss. Experimentally, using an acoustic platform with electrically tunable loss, we not only directly observe the coalescence of eigenenergies but also the coalescence of eigenstates, offering a complete verification of the ET-BIC formation. The triply synergistic ET-BICs may pave the way for wave devices that simultaneously demand robustness, sensitivity, and BIC confinement.
item.dc:creator: Luohong Liu, Qicheng Zhang, Shuaishuai Tong, Chunyin Qiu

item.title: Pelletization Pressure Engineering of the Superconducting Properties of Fluorine-Doped PrFeAsO
item.description: arXiv:2611.10083v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We investigate the influence of the pelletization pressure on the structural, microstructural, and superconducting properties of fluorine-doped PrFeAsO0.7F0.3 (Pr1111). Precursor powders are pressed into pellets at pressures ranging from 174 to 1131 MPa, after which the applied pressure is released and all samples undergo an identical two-step conventional synthesis process at ambient pressure (CSP-AP). All samples predominantly exhibit the tetragonal P4/nmm structure, and the lattice parameter a and unit-cell volume V decrease with increasing pelletization pressure up to an intermediate-pressure range (~900 MPa) before increasing at higher pressures. The actual fluorine-content derived from energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) also increase with pelletization pressure, while Raman spectra show only modest variations in the characteristic vibrational modes associated with Fe and As. The superconducting response exhibits a non-monotonic dependence on the pelletization pressure. Among the investigated samples, the sample pelletized at 870 MPa exhibits the most favorable overall superconducting properties, with a superconducting onset temperature of 44.2 K, ~5 K higher than that of the lowest-pressure sample. It also displays a narrower superconducting transition, the highest relative sample density, a favorable effective magnetic critical current density at high fields, and a relatively large effective thermally activated flux-flow activation energy. At higher pelletization pressures, the superconducting response deteriorates, coinciding with increases in the lattice parameters, increased secondary-phase contributions, and reduced relative density. These findings establish the pelletization pressure as a relevant processing parameter for modifying the structural, microstructural and superconducting properties of Pr1111 during CSP-AP.
item.dc:creator: Jayant Kumar, Konrad Kwatek, Tatiana Zajarniuk, Taras Palasyuk, Yaroslaw Konopelnyk, Tomasz Cetner, Cezariusz Jastrz\k{e}bski, Shiv J. Singh

item.title: Engineering a digital acoustic black hole
item.description: arXiv:2611.10540v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We show how to design and build an analogue black hole as a synchronous digital circuit. We define the sound speed, the flow and the horizon of such a circuit in terms of its own logic, and realise one on a field-programmable gate array, where the black hole is probed electrically with a signal generator and an oscilloscope. We measure the stability of the horizon, its causal cone, the ringdown and rotational superradiance. A single flipped bit inside the horizon leaks out by an amount that falls exponentially with depth. Digital circuits thus form a reconfigurable class of gravitational analogues and realise an analogue black hole as a cellular automaton.
item.dc:creator: Antonino Flachi

item.title: Lifting mechanical zero modes without dispersion
item.description: arXiv:2611.10937v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Floppy frameworks carry flat bands of zero-frequency mechanisms with no finite-frequency resonance, and couplings that lift them usually spread them. We show that an on-site tensor lifts a mechanism band without first-order dispersion exactly when, projected onto the mechanisms, it acts as wavevector-independent scalars on orthogonal pieces. Three structures achieve this: local normal modes, invariant symmetry sectors, and a balance law. A mechanism moves both ends of every bond between two vertex classes equally along it, and where the inter-class bond tensors are class scalars this balance law fixes its norm shares and hence the flat value from geometry alone. For the fluorite net the band lies outside the tensor spectrum, at 14/9 of the contact stiffness to first order, and stays flat to all orders in a fixed cage. A placement inside a tiling dual that keeps the common symmetry supplies such tensors, because each contact star inherits its site symmetry. Ten catalogued dual pairs lift flat; half are eigenvalue cases a resolved count matches, and the balance law explains flat bands in random cages too. Duality makes the rigid cage common. In a printable beam-frame lattice, contacts that lock joint rotation remove first-order bending dispersion whenever bonded mechanisms are orthogonal local normals.
item.dc:creator: Joohan Nam

item.title: HydroTuring: A physics probe benchmark testing mass, energy, and momentum conservation in hydrologic models
item.description: arXiv:2611.11563v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Hydrologic models, including deep learning systems now deployed for operational flood forecasting, are evaluated primarily by how closely their simulated hydrographs match observed streamflow. However, high hydrograph skill does not guarantee physical consistency: in a synthetic calibration experiment, a conceptual model that loses 15% of its water input to an unreported sink still reaches a Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency of 0.93, and no shared benchmark tests whether models obey fundamental conservation laws. Here we introduce HydroTuring (v0.1.0), a black-box benchmark of 37 physics probes that test mass (24 probes), energy (7) and momentum (6) conservation in hydrologic models. Each probe runs a controlled experiment on forcing generated at run time from a recorded seed and applies binary pass or fail criteria validated against 18 physically exact and 59 deliberately broken reference models. Across 32 evaluated models (3 exact references, 7 AI-based models and 22 process-based models), only the 3 exact references pass every probe among the 28 models scored on 5 or more probes. Process-based and AI-based models pass similar shares of their scored probes (76% and 74%), and a pre-trained flood-forecasting LSTM fails 6 of the 11 runoff-only probes it can be scored on. Furthermore, 49% of all 1,184 model-probe pairs remain unscored because models omit the required state or flux variables, while the scored failures occur in perturbation responses and state bounds rather than long-term water-budget closure. HydroTuring provides a reproducible smoke test for model development, peer review and operational deployment under an open community protocol.
item.dc:creator: Zhi Li, Changming Li, Siavash Shams, Han Wang, Qingyi Yang, Yuanhang Liu, Taiqi Lian, Xin Lan, Shunan Zhou, Binlan Zhang, Siddik Barbhuiya, Songkun Yan, Bing Li, Jinlong Hu, Yaji Wang, Zhenjiang Wu, Mofan Zhang, Kaihao Long, Jingzhi Chen, Yuan-Heng Wang

item.title: Scalable Bayesian Optimization for Efficient Exploration of Moire Patterns
item.description: arXiv:2611.12010v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large materials design spaces often contain rare high-performing configurations that are difficult to identify through trial-and-error exploration or purely representative machine-learning (ML) sampling. In this work, we present FruBO, a flexible Bayesian Optimization framework for accelerating the discovery of optimal configurations in computationally demanding materials design problems. As a case study, we investigate multilayer Moir\'e patterns generated by the superposition of six rotated hexagonal lattices, where the objective is to identify the rotational conformation that maximizes pore-size uniformity, quantified using the Jain fairness index. The resulting benchmark contains 600,000 unique configurations and exhibits a highly skewed objective distribution, making the global optimum difficult to locate by random sampling. We compare random exploration, Gaussian Process-based Bayesian Optimization, and Bayesian Optimization using a lightweight CatBoost surrogate with committee-based uncertainty estimation. Random sampling identifies the global optimum only after 533,012 evaluations, requiring approximately 31 hours, while Gaussian Process-based BO becomes impractical due to GPU memory exhaustion after 290 acquired samples. In contrast, FruBO with CatBoost identifies the global optimum after 1,470 acquired samples and approximately 1.15 hours. These results demonstrate that scalable surrogate models can substantially improve the feasibility and efficiency of BO in large nanomaterials design spaces.
item.dc:creator: Panagiotis Krokidas, Christos Lazaridis, Vassilis Sioros, Efi-Maria Papia, Vassilios Constantoudis, George Giannakopoulos

item.title: Why fluid relaxation modes matter: Nonlinear frequency response, dynamical integrity, and dynamic pull-in of electrostatic microbeams with squeeze-film damping
item.description: arXiv:2611.12350v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The squeeze film between an electrostatically actuated microbeam can both induce damping and add stiffness to the structure. In addition, the dynamics of the film can interact with the nonlinear response of the microbeam. This paper extends a reduced-order model built on the complex modes of the coupled fluid-structure problem to the computation of periodic responses and their stability for clamped-clamped microbeams. Periodic orbits are continued in the frequency domain, and their stability is determined from their Floquet multipliers. The robustness of the response is assessed through basins of attraction, integrity measures, and dynamic pull-in maps in the plane of the excitation parameters. The model is validated against the measured and computed frequency response of a microswitch. Closed-form expressions are derived for the fluid relaxation modes, together with a correction for strongly coupled films, and define a parameter that characterizes the regime of the film. The approach is applied to different microbeams including cases where fluid modes relax on the timescale of the oscillation. For all simulated devices, a single fluid mode is necessary and sufficient, whereas adding coupled modes cannot replace it, whether the fluid modes respond quasi-statically or carry their own dynamics. Removing the fluid mode displaces both bifurcations that bound the pull-in band, changes the size of the basins of attraction and the position of the attractor within them, misses an abrupt erosion of the safe basin under increasing excitation, and shifts the whole region of dynamic pull-in in the excitation plane. The reduced model, with three real unknowns, makes these global analyses affordable for a fully coupled fluid-structure system.
item.dc:creator: Fehmi Najar

item.title: Scalable operating currents in amorphous W-N/FePt superconducting rectifiers
item.description: arXiv:2611.12476v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We demonstrate high-efficiency, field-free superconducting diode behavior in W-N/FePt bilayers fabricated entirely by sputtering at room temperature. The devices combine amorphous W-N superconducting thin films with a 48-nm-thick FePt layer exhibiting remanent stripe-domain magnetization. We used lithographically patterned microbridges to compare W-N/FePt bilayers with single-layer W-N reference films at three nominal W-N thicknesses (18, 24, and 28 nm). The bilayers exhibit superconducting transition temperatures of approximately 4.1-4.3 K. At zero applied magnetic field, the current-voltage (I-V) characteristics exhibit pronounced nonreciprocity, controlled by the orientation of the in-plane remanent FePt magnetization relative to the transport current. The diode response is maximized for perpendicular alignment, reverses polarity upon magnetization reversal, and is strongly suppressed when the magnetization is aligned with the current. This behavior is consistent with asymmetric vortex entry and motion governed by the magnetic stray fields generated near the bridge edges. At 3 K with the remanent magnetization perpendicular to the current, increasing the W-N thickness from 18 to 28 nm widens the current interval between the dissipation thresholds for opposite polarities from about 0.3 to 1.55 mA. All three bilayers exhibit diode efficiencies of approximately 75-80% in this configuration.
item.dc:creator: S. Russo, A. Sanson, Yeonkyu Lee, Jeehoon Kim, N. Haberkorn

item.title: Spin-valve effect through electrostatic coupling
item.description: arXiv:2611.12588v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We propose a spin-valve effect in which an insulating magnetic van der Waals multilayer controls the conductance of an adjacent non-magnetic conductor by electrostatic coupling, without transport-electrons entering the magnetic layers. The coupling is induced by the variations of the electronic structure when the relative orientation of the magnetization of adjacent monolayers changes from parallel to antiparallel, modifying both the dielectric constant and band alignment. We consider two types of coupling and device concepts: charge transfer to a graphene monolayer and capacitive coupling in a single-electron transistor. We use density functional calculations to assess the magnitude of the effect in various materials, including CrI$_3$, CrBr$_3$, CrCl$_3$ and NiBr$_2$. We predict magnetoresistance ratios in the range of 1.14-1.20 for the charge-transfer device and up to $10^3$ in the single-electron transistor.
item.dc:creator: Jan Phillips, Joaqu\'in Fern\'andez-Rossier

item.title: g4chargeit: Geant4-based kinetic Monte Carlo simulations of charging in dielectric materials
item.description: arXiv:2602.17332v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present g4chargeit, a kinetic Monte Carlo framework built on Geant4 for self-consistent simulation of time-dependent electrostatic charging in dielectric materials. The model explicitly incorporates stochastic particle transport and scattering processes using validated Geant4 cross-sections, while self-consistently evolving the electric potential and field. As a representative application, we simulate the charging of regolith grains under average dayside conditions on the Moon. The surface of the Moon, in addition to other airless planetary bodies, are regularly exposed to solar ultraviolet photons and solar-wind plasma, creating a radiation environment in which electrostatic interactions among regolith grains become significant. Until now, simulations of regolith charging have often relied on analytical approximations that oversimplify grain geometry and interaction mechanisms. Our Geant4-based simulations reveal charge accumulation within intergrain micro-cavities, leading to repulsive electrostatic forces consistent with experimental observations. The framework establishes a multiscale approach that links microscopic scattering events to the continuity equation of surface charge density and to the formation of macroscopic surface charge patches in complex grain geometries. Although demonstrated here for planetary regolith, the method is general and applicable to a broad range of dielectric charging problems. The code is openly available at https://github.com/kgandhi63/g4chargeit.git.
item.dc:creator: Kush P. Gandhi, Advik D. Vira, William M. Farrell, Nikolai Simonov, Alvaro Romero-Calvo, Thomas M. Orlando, Phillip N. First, Zhigang Jiang

item.title: Vibe-FDTR: An agent-oriented framework for reproducible frequency-domain thermoreflectance data analysis
item.description: arXiv:2607.28200v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Frequency-domain thermoreflectance (FDTR) is a laser pump-probe technique widely used to measure thermal properties at the micro- and nanoscale; however, it relies on a complex data analysis procedure that demands substantial domain expertise and is susceptible to subtle human errors. Here, we present Vibe-FDTR, an agent-oriented framework that enables large language model (LLM) agents to perform reliable and reproducible FDTR analyses directly from natural language requests. This framework couples a configuration-driven FDTR code package, which enforces physical and parametric consistency, with procedural agent skills that translate user intentions into organized and verifiable analysis steps. We evaluate Vibe-FDTR using a controlled benchmark with two levels: synthetic single-step tasks and real-data multi-step tasks based on measurements of gold-coated graphite samples. Across the two levels, agents using Vibe-FDTR achieve success rates of 100% and 98.9%, respectively. In sharp contrast, ablating skills (Code-agent) reduces performance to 91.4% and 36.7%, which drops further to 38.6% and 0% when the domain package is also omitted (Agent-only). Beyond success rate, Vibe-FDTR also reduces computational cost by 87.7% relative to the Code-agent variant and cuts execution time by more than 60%. Finally, an optional expert mode supports experimental planning via autonomous sensitivity and uncertainty evaluations, and formulates physically grounded recommendations for underspecified tasks. These results demonstrate that encapsulating domain code and expert knowledge into agent skills offers a promising route toward low-barrier, autonomous, and trustworthy thermal metrology.
item.dc:creator: Fuwei Yang, Weiheng Li, Bai Song

item.title: Light in Slices: How to Enable Precise Laser Processing?
item.description: arXiv:2509.22665v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Ultrashort (femtosecond, fs) laser pulses have fascinating properties as they allow to confine optical energy on extreme scales in space and time. Such fs-laser pulsed beams can be seen as spatially thin slices of intense light that are radially and axially constrained to the micrometer scale, while simultaneously propagating at the extremely high speed of light. Their high peak intensities and their short time lapse makes such laser pulses unique tools for materials processing, as their duration is shorter than the time required to transfer absorbed optical energy, via electron-phonon coupling, from the electronic system of the solid to its lattice. Hence, the laser pulse energy remains localized during the interaction and does not spread via diffusion into the area surrounding the irradiated region. As one consequence, the fs-laser thus offers increased precision for material modification or ablation accompanied by a reduced heat-affected zone of only a few hundred nanometers. On the other hand, the high laser peak intensities can enable nonlinear material interactions that are rendering unique material excitation and relaxation pathways possible. In this chapter, we briefly review the reasons for the enormous success of ultrashort pulse lasers in materials processing - both for the processing of the surface or in the bulk of solids. We identify the underlying fundamental processes that can limit the precision or the up-scaling of the laser processing towards large volumes, areas, or processing rates. Strategies to overcome such limitations will be outlined and questions on the ultimate limits of laser material processing will be answered.
item.dc:creator: Stefan Nolte, J\"orn Bonse, Nadezhda M. Bulgakova

item.title: On deep squeezing or cooling a parametric resonator using feedback
item.description: arXiv:2602.21847v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Here we analyze ways to achieve deep subthreshold squeezing or cooling of fluctuations in a parametric resonator enhanced by a lock-in amplifier feedback loop. The main advance and novelty of this paper is that we analyzed the full impact of this feedback on the response of the parametric resonator to an ac drive or to additive noise. Due to this feedback, the dynamics of the parametric resonator becomes more complex and, in addition to a saddle-node bifurcation (SNB), a Hopf bifurcation (HB) at the instability threshold can also occur. We calculate the phase-dependent amplification gain in the response of the resonator to an added ac signal with three independent techniques: approximately using the averaging method (AM) or the harmonic balance method (HBM), and more precisely using Floquet theory (FT) and Green's functions. The HB was predicted by the AM, FT, and a modified version of the HBM that takes into account quasi-periodicity. In our analysis of fluctuations, we were able to calculate the noise spectral density and the squeezing or cooling of fluctuations using Fourier techniques and FT. Deamplification and cooling occur near the HB, whereas deep squeezing and heating occur near a SNB. Furthermore, we show that there is an optimal amount of parametric pumping and feedback to reach the strongest cooling. The theoretical framework presented here is general and could be applied to a wide range of physical implementations.
item.dc:creator: Adriano A. Batista, Raoni S. N. Moreira, A. A. Lisboa de Souza

item.title: Advances in electrical contacts to single crystals of emerging materials for transport measurements
item.description: arXiv:2606.00173v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Transport measurements that probe electrical resistivity of a material under varying external stimuli, such as temperature, magnetic field, optical illumination, and gate voltage, are among the most important experimental techniques in condensed matter physics. These measurements provide critical insights into the fundamental electronic properties of materials. In recent years, they have facilitated the discovery and exploration of intriguing physical phenomena (e.g., superconductivity and quantum oscillations) and unique device functionalities (e.g., photoresponse and electrostatic gating effects) in various emerging materials, particularly in the form of single crystals. However, unlike large-scale wafers or thin films, newly synthesized single crystals often pose substantial challenges in establishing reliable electrical contacts due to their irregular geometries, limited dimensions, inherent structural characteristics, and potential susceptibility to degradation. In this review, we highlight recent technological advancements in the fabrication of high-quality, lithographically defined multi-terminal electrodes on both exfoliable and non-exfoliable single crystals for transport measurements. Our work provides a practical guide for researchers seeking to select appropriate contact-fabrication strategies tailored to unique characteristics of emerging crystals.
item.dc:creator: Huandong Chen, Abhay N. Pasupathy, Jayakanth Ravichandran

item.title: From populations to absolute binding affinities in molecular simulations: exact volumetric terms and practical estimators
item.description: arXiv:2608.04834v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Biomolecular simulations of binding commonly confine the unbound ligand with volumetric restraints to accelerate convergence. However, a general account of how such restraints enter the volumetric term of the standard binding free energy, and of how this term should be evaluated from histogram data, is currently lacking. We take as our starting point the established relation, in the dilute limit, between the binding constant $K$ and the relative populations of the bound and unbound states, which we re-derive from the canonical partition function of molecular solutes in explicit solvent. Building on this relation, we show that a restraint that leaves the bound state unaffected and confines a homogeneous unbound region modifies the volumetric term in a single way, by replacing the system volume with the volume of the region over which the unbound population is evaluated. This yields closed-form estimators for restrained simulations, computable from histograms of any suitably defined reaction coordinate, with the volumetric term kept explicit. Previous expressions based on the potential of mean force are recovered as a special case. The analysis also exposes two distinct errors in current practice: single-bin estimators, which reduce the bound state to one histogram bin and are not valid estimators of $K$, and working formulas that omit the bin width entering the volumetric term, which make the result depend on the unit of length. We apply the estimators to a Lennard-Jones dimer, the cucurbit[7]uril/1-adamantanol host--guest complex, and the galactonate--DgoT ligand--protein complex.
item.dc:creator: Davide Mandelli, Emiliano Ippoliti, Charles Plate

item.title: Broad-angle photon-pair generation from high-$Q$ flatband resonant 3R-MoS$_{2}$ metasurfaces
item.description: arXiv:2609.07082v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) in ultrathin optical resonant metasurfaces offers a promising platform for integrated quantum light sources. However, conventional resonances suffer from steep momentum dispersion, limiting photon-pair generation to narrow excitation and emission angles. Here, we demonstrate a high-$Q$ flatband resonant 3R-MoS$_{2}$ metasurface for high-efficiency, broad-angle SPDC photon-pair generation. By combining Brillouin zone folding with in-plane symmetry breaking, we engineer a high-$Q$ flatband resonance in the near-infrared regime, maintaining a robust $Q$-factor across a wide range of incident angles. Exploiting the strong local electric field enhancement of resonance and the large second-order susceptibility of 3R-MoS$_{2}$, the metasurface boosts the degenerate SPDC pair-generation rate with orders of magnitude enhancement over an unpatterned film of identical thickness. Crucially, the near-zero band dispersion extends the effective emission angle to $\pm 5^{\circ}$ with negligible spectral drift $\sim 0.1$ nm and high directional tolerance. Under pulsed excitation with a finite spectral bandwidth, the metasurface maintains a substantial bandwidth-averaged photon-pair yield, while demonstrating strong spectral locking of the resonant emission channel against pump wavelength detuning despite the expected trade-off in generation efficiency. This work establishes a versatile strategy for momentum-independent quantum light sources, opening new avenues for scan-free quantum ghost imaging and quantum information processing.
item.dc:creator: Tingting Liu, Huifu Qiu, Xintong Shi, Jumin Qiu, Shuyuan Xiao

item.title: An information circuit driven by a skyrmion Maxwell's demon
item.description: arXiv:2609.36955v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: At the nanoscale, observation and feedback may transform thermal fluctuations into valuable resources. Nevertheless, a framework for experimentation with the resulting probability currents has yet to be firmly established. Here, we present an information heat engine incorporating two interacting magnetic skyrmions in adjacent potential wells. Feedback from a skyrmion in Brownian motion at room temperature to the other yields a Maxwell's demon and a circulating probability current in their joint state space. A linear relationship is confirmed between the probability current and the information affinity, the thermodynamic conjugate value, within certain response range and conditions. We identify the slope as the "information conductance" analogous to electrical conductance. The information conductance is modified by skyrmion interactions and scattering, while Kirchhoff's laws remain valid. These results establish a circuit representation of the state space of an information heat engine with potential applications to computing devices, biological systems and chemical reactions.
item.dc:creator: Soma Miki, Yoshishige Suzuki, Ryo Ishikawa, Yuki Hibino, Shunya Morishita, Hiroto Imanishi, Keigo Adachi, Yoichi Shiota, Takayuki Nozaki, Minori Goto, Hikaru Nomura, Shigemi Mizukami, Eiiti Tamura

item.title: Imaging the topological sign of a Dirac mass with spin-polarized tunneling
item.description: arXiv:2610.17464v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A Dirac mass is characterized not only by its magnitude but also by its sign, which influences the Berry curvature, Hall response, and the propagation direction of chiral boundary modes. However, local spectroscopy of magnetic topological surfaces has so far accessed only the gap magnitude $|M|$. Here we show how the topological sign of $M$ can be determined locally. We first establish the sign information that spin-resolved tunneling can access and the reference required to obtain an absolute Hall sign. Although spin--orbital entanglement generally obscures the relation between measured spin and Dirac pseudospin, crystalline rotation symmetry alleviates this ambiguity at the band edge. On a $C_3$ axis, an axial tip couples to a fully spin-polarized state whose tunneling asymmetry directly reveals the sign of the occupied-band Berry curvature, independent of orbital composition. We further show that the zeroth Landau level provides an independent mass-sign measurement with an unpolarized tip, while opposite domains and their chiral domain-wall modes provide self-consistency checks. These results pave the way for imaging the locations where the topological character changes within a material, rather than merely identifying where a spectral gap appears.
item.dc:creator: Payman Kazemikhah, Ruolun Zhang, Byunghoon Kim, Xiangyu Luo, Zachary Ducorsky, Yu-Peng Zhu, Md. Shafayat Hossain, M. Zahid Hasan

item.title: The Extended Diode Equation
item.description: arXiv:2610.32090v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: For more than seven decades, the p-n junction current-voltage characteristic has been derived by treating majority carriers as an inert background and conflating the junction voltage with the applied bias. Here we show that the base electric field, generated by the coupling of excess majority and minority carriers, fundamentally alters the internal potential distribution. This self-consistent framework yields a closed-form extended diode equation that reproduces the high-injection roll-off without invoking an external series resistance, thereby eliminating an empirical patch that has persisted in the classical theory.
item.dc:creator: Jianhong Yang, Gonghao Sun, Tinglan Li

item.title: A Self-Consistent Two-Carrier Drift-Diffusion Framework for p-n Junctions: Extended Diode Equation, Power Dissipation, and Base Transit Time
item.description: arXiv:2610.32112v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The classical theory of p-n junctions derives the current-voltage characteristic from minority-carrier diffusion alone: majority carriers are treated as an inert background, the quasi-neutral base as field-free, and the junction voltage as equal to the applied bias. These premises fail together under high bias and high-level injection, where the observed current roll-off is reproduced only by appending an empirical series resistance outside the junction physics. Here we develop a self-consistent two-carrier drift-diffusion framework that introduces no assumption beyond the classical ones. Excess majority carriers are shown to be electrostatically forced transport participants: the ambipolar diffusion equation, closed by exact two-sided boundary conditions, yields a unified excess-carrier profile. The resulting base field separates into an ohmic and a Dember component, and all four current components follow in closed form, their sum being position independent. At device level the framework closes into an extended diode equation that contains the Shockley equation as its low-injection, long-base limit and reproduces the n=2 roll-off intrinsically. The junction voltage emerges as a self-limiting drop confined to the space-charge region and separated from the applied bias by exact base drops. Two device-level corrections are quantified: at high current, 75-90% of the dissipation migrates from the junction into the quasi-neutral base, and field-assisted acceleration shortens the base transit time by up to a factor of six. Three parameter-free predictions follow: a universal ideality-factor crossover that passes through 3/2 when the boundary excess equals the doping, a high-injection onset voltage that scales as 119 mV per decade of doping, and a geometry factor that survives into high injection.
item.dc:creator: Jianhong Yang, Tinglan Li, Gonghao Sun
